title: Dance of the Octopus and music ahead of its time
summary: A good statement is good; Red's genius was as a composer.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: It's funny you should mention that. I was talking to my

roommate yesterday, who is a very good jazz drummer and just overall a very aware person musically and otherwise, and I was telling him about Red Norvo's recording of "Dance of the Octopus" which he has never heard, and I told him that here is something that was recorded in 1933 and it sounds like--my own words were, it was years ahead of its time. My roommate's reply was, well you know, music isn't like that, it isn't ahead of its time. A good musical statement is a good musical statement.

Some people have a vision and a spark of genius, because it's the genius that pulls the whole thing together, that gives it validity. Genius doesn't necessarily live or last for a lifetime; it can come in spurts and this was obviously one of those times.
ing that instrument, it really was the composer and they haven't heard anything like it since.
It really is something; it was a mark in my life. In my early parts, as far as the jazz scene was concerned, that and Ellington did it. In my awareness stage.
Don't you still think you're in an awareness stage?

Yes. Well, when I say that I meant consciously aware, because as I said I hedged and I had to hedge because I had to think of all those years sitting alongside the radio and whatever record player we had, playing the drums and trumpet.
This was all the while I was growing up, during the earlier school years, so that had to do something. But I wasn't consciously listening or thinking, and that's the best way.
Perhaps at a certain time I think that's true.
I think what's important is we associated with our associates; it's a social art, a very social art. You can't do it alone, you can't do it locked in a closet.
